description: Rick follows seafood cultures from Cornwall to Naples, Goa, Galicia, Australia, the Chesapeake, Thailand and Yorkshire, looking at how local catches, markets and techniques produce radically different food from the same basic relationship with the sea.

s02e00.description: A practical fish-cookery masterclass in which Rick demonstrates the fundamentals behind his seafood kitchen, from preparing mussels and picking crab to filleting fish, making lemon-sole goujons, handling salmon and grilling cleanly.

s02e01.description: From the North Sea coast to Naples, Rick compares the directness of Suffolk cod and Thames brown shrimp with southern Italian seafood, sauces and the exuberant fish cooking of the Bay of Naples.

s02e02.description: Goa supplies prawn caldine, lobster and spice before Rick returns to Cornwall, where turbot cooked with cider and cream shows how local fish can absorb influences without losing its character.

s02e03.description: In Galicia, Rick encounters percebes, hake and clams before looking back to British shellfish and the theatrical Cornish tradition of stargazy pie.

s02e04.description: Goan shark vindaloo and dhal give way to the Chesapeake, where oysters and crab cakes reveal another seafood culture; back in Cornwall, Rick folds those travels into a mackerel nasi goreng.

s02e05.description: Australian cooks demonstrate confident handling of abundant seafood before Rick returns to European flavours and prepares seared tuna in Padstow, connecting technique rather than geography.

s02e06.description: The Chesapeake brings striped bass, oyster shacks and a deeply local fishing culture, while Rick translates the journey into the kind of straightforward seafood cooking that works back in Cornwall.

s02e07.description: Hua Hin's markets and Thai kitchens supply red curry, jasmine rice and fish-ball ideas, which Rick carries home into delicate poached fish and pasta rather than treating the trip as mere exotic garnish.

s02e08.description: Soft-shell crab and lobster in America lead through Singapore-style chilli crab to Whitby, where the odyssey ends with Britain's most democratic seafood institution: fish and chips.
